title: Detect Squares
description:
Store points on an integer grid and count axis-aligned squares that use a query point as one corner.

Implement the DetectSquares class:

  • __init__() creates an empty multiset of points.
  • add(point: list[int]) -> None adds one occurrence of the point [x, y], even if it already exists.
  • count(point: list[int]) -> int counts squares of positive area with the query point as one corner and three stored point occurrences as the other corners.

Only axis-aligned squares count: the sides must be parallel to the coordinate axes and have equal positive length. The query point need not have been added. Repeated stored points count with multiplicity: multiply the numbers of occurrences at the other three corners for each possible square.

You are graded on a recorded sequence of calls on one live object. The first call names the class and passes constructor arguments; subsequent calls name methods and their arguments. The constructor and methods returning nothing report null; the result array has one entry per call.

Constraints:

  • Each coordinate is an integer from 0 to 1000.
  • At most 3000 add and count calls.

Example 1:

Calls: ["DetectSquares","add","add","add","count","add","count"]
Arguments: [[],[[3,10]],[[11,2]],[[3,2]],[[11,10]],[[11,2]],[[11,10]]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,1,null,2]

The first query has one square; duplicating the diagonal corner at (11,2) makes two.

Example 2:

Calls: ["DetectSquares","add","add","add","count","count"]
Arguments: [[],[[0,0]],[[0,2]],[[2,0]],[[2,2]],[[0,0]]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,1,0]

Querying (2,2) closes the square, but querying (0,0) lacks its opposite corner as a stored point.

Example 3:

Calls: ["DetectSquares","add","add","add","add","count","count"]
Arguments: [[],[[1,1]],[[1,1]],[[2,1]],[[1,2]],[[2,2]],[[2,1]]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,null,2,0]

The duplicate corner at (1,1) yields two squares for (2,2); (2,1) cannot form one.

A query point alone never makes a square.
Collinear diagonal points cannot form an axis-aligned square.
The three stored corners form one square with the query point.
A stored copy of the query point is not substituted for a different corner.
Two copies at each of two corners multiply to four squares.
The requested corner closes the larger square only when all its three remaining corners exist.
Points at the upper coordinate boundary can complete a positive-area square.
